lesson.title: Island of Hope, Island of Tears: Processing America's Newcomers
lesson.summary: From 1892 until 1954, Ellis Island in New York Harbor served as the nation's main gateway for immigration, processing millions of newcomers, most of them part of the new immigration wave from southern and eastern Europe.
lesson.body:
Ellis Island opened as a federal immigration station on January 1, 1892, replacing New York's earlier immigrant landing depot at Castle Garden. The change reflected the growing scale and complexity of immigration, especially the new immigration wave from southern and eastern Europe, which required more standardized, federally run processing than the old state run system could handle.

The very first immigrant processed at the new station was a teenager from County Cork, Ireland, named Annie Moore, who arrived on opening day.

Passengers who could afford first or second class tickets were typically inspected briefly aboard their ships and rarely needed to pass through Ellis Island at all. The great majority of immigrants, however, traveled in steerage, the cheapest class of passage, packed tightly below deck, and were ferried to the island for processing. There, officials conducted a medical inspection, checking for contagious diseases and visible signs of illness, and a legal inspection, verifying identity, destination, and financial means. The overwhelming majority passed through in only a few hours, but a small percentage, roughly two percent, were ultimately denied entry, and some families were separated in the process, which is part of why Ellis Island earned the nickname island of hope, island of tears.

Immigration on the West Coast worked very differently. Angel Island, which opened in San Francisco Bay in 1910, processed mostly Asian immigrants under far harsher and more suspicious conditions, shaped by discriminatory laws such as the Chinese Exclusion Act, and detentions there could stretch on for weeks or months rather than hours.

By the time it closed in 1954, Ellis Island had processed more than 12 million immigrants, and a very large share of Americans today can trace at least one ancestor through its records.
